evals.prompt: Define information architecture in 2-3 sentences. Include navigation, hierarchy, labeling, wayfinding, and findability.
expected_elements: Structures information so users can find and understand it
Includes navigation or page hierarchy
Includes labeling systems
Includes wayfinding or cross-links
Optimizes for user tasks and findability

evals.prompt: Explain the mental model for information architecture: why should top tasks drive structure before implementation categories?
expected_elements: Starts from user goals or top tasks
Inventories content or screens
Groups by user goal before implementation detail
Avoids promoting every important thing to top-level navigation
Uses structure to make paths obvious

evals.prompt: Distinguish information-architecture from taxonomy-design, layout-composition, design-system-architecture, microcopy, and a11y. Give mechanism-level boundaries.
expected_elements: taxonomy-design owns classification governance and assignment rules
layout-composition owns structure inside a page or screen
design-system-architecture owns component and token systems
microcopy owns sentence-level wording
a11y owns accessibility compliance and assistive technology behavior
information-architecture owns navigation, hierarchy, grouping, and wayfinding

evals.prompt: A teammate says, 'This feature is important, so it must be a top-level navigation item.' Use information architecture to correct the misconception.
expected_elements: Importance alone does not determine top-level navigation
Frequency, task entry points, and findability matter
A tab, section, filter, or cross-link may be better
Labels should use recognizable user language
Structure should be tested against task scenarios

evals.prompt: A documentation site has setup, troubleshooting, billing, and admin-role pages scattered across product-feature categories. Users cannot find setup instructions. Apply information architecture and recommend the first changes.
expected_elements: Names setup as a top task or primary entry point
Inventories current content
Groups content by user goal rather than product internals
Creates a clearer navigation/page hierarchy or setup hub
Adds cross-links or wayfinding from related pages
Tests the structure against no-prior-knowledge task prompts
